transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. It's really good to meet you, too. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me. 

Um... well, I hope I'm explaining this right, but... I guess I've just been feeling kind of like I'm constantly running on a motor lately? I mean, I like to stay productive, which is normally a good thing, right? But I'll finish one thing at school—I teach special education—or I'll finish a task at home, and I just... I immediately jump right into the next thing. It's like I can't ever really shut myself off. 

I really don't want to sound like I'm complaining, because I love my job and my life, I just... I want to make sure I'm doing my best for my students and not wearing people out. Does that make sense? I hope that's the kind of information you were looking for.
When you're feeling this driven, do you need less sleep than usual?

Oh, gosh, no... I don't think so. I mean, I definitely still need my sleep! I'm not staying up all night or anything drastic like that. 

I really try to be responsible and keep a good routine so I'm fully present for my students the next day, you know? So by the time evening rolls around, I'm actually pretty ready for bed. I usually get a completely normal amount of rest... I hope that's a good sign? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of answers. But yes, I definitely still need a full night's sleep.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t a clear reason to?

Oh, worrying? Um... no, I don't really think so. I mean, obviously, I care a lot about my students and want them to do well, so I focus on that, but I don't sit around agonizing over things for no reason. 

I really try to be a very positive person, you know? It's so important for the kids that I keep an upbeat attitude and a good environment for them. So, no, my mind isn't really filled with worries or anything like that... it's just more that my brain is always... going? If that makes sense? 

I hope I'm giving you the right kind of answers. Am I explaining that okay?
During these times, do you actually feel unusually upbeat or high?

Oh, unusually upbeat or high? Um... no, definitely not. I mean, I'm a cheerful person by nature, and I really try to bring a lot of energy to the classroom because my students respond so well to that. But I wouldn't say I feel... high, or anything extreme like that. 

I just like to keep things moving and stay positive. I really wouldn't want anyone to think I was acting inappropriately or out of control at work, you know? I take my job very seriously. It's just a normal, happy mood, I think... just maybe a little more restless than I'd like. Does that sound like what you're asking about? I want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture.
Do you often have trouble staying focused on one task?

Trouble staying focused? Um... well, I wouldn't say I have *trouble*, exactly. I mean, as a special education teacher, I'm juggling a lot of different things at once—IEP meetings, lesson plans, working with the kids one-on-one—so I kind of *have* to bounce around from task to task. 

I think I'm actually pretty good at multitasking! I really try my best to stay on top of everything because I don't want to let my students or my colleagues down. Sometimes I might start grading a paper and then remember I need to prep an activity, so I switch over... but I always get it all done eventually. I'm very dedicated to my work. 

I wouldn't want you to think I'm not doing my job well or anything. Is it normal to jump between tasks when you have a busy schedule like mine? I hope that makes sense... I just want to make sure I'm answering this the way you need me to.
Do you feel a strong need for things to be done in a very exact or perfect way?

Exact or perfect? Um... no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, I definitely care about doing my job well, of course! But I don't need things to be, you know, perfectly rigid or anything like that. 

Especially working in special education, you kind of have to be flexible and just... go with the flow, right? I'd hate to be so strict about having things done an exact way that I ended up making my students uncomfortable or stressed out. So I really try to be very adaptable and just keep things moving. 

I hope that's a good trait to have... I mean, does that sound like a healthy way to approach things? I just want to make sure I'm doing right by the kids, you know?
Looking back to when you were a child, were you already the kind of person who always felt restless or constantly on the go?

Oh, as a child? Um... well, yes, I suppose I've always had a lot of energy. My mother actually used to joke that even back in elementary school, I was the one teaching the class from my seat. I was just... very enthusiastic, I guess. I was always popping out of my chair, or, um, talking and chiming in before the teacher had even finished giving directions. 

I really didn't mean to be disruptive, I promise! I just got so excited and wanted to be involved. But yes, that's just... that's always been a part of who I am, long before adulthood. It definitely isn't something that just started recently with, you know, the changes in my family. 

I hope that doesn't make me sound like I was a bad kid or anything... I really always wanted to be good for my teachers, which is probably why I became one! Does that make sense? Being that eager to participate as a child? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right history.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports a longstanding hyperactive/impulsive pattern beginning in childhood, characterized by feeling constantly 'on a motor,' chronic restlessness, excessive energy, popping out of her chair as a child, and blurting/talking before instructions were finished. Symptoms are not better explained by mania, generalized anxiety, or obsessive-compulsive/perfectionistic concerns based on explicit denials of decreased need for sleep, elevated/high mood, excessive worry, and rigid perfectionism. While inattentive symptoms and full impairment details were not comprehensively established, the available evidence most strongly supports ADHD, unspecified presentation.
